evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in regions with strong service-sector demand low-skilled employment levels via automation substitution]

[PATH:empirical] Difference-in-differences analysis of minimum wage increases in U.S. states with high service-sector employment (e.g., Washington, California) matched to automation adoption rates in fast-food and retail from Bureau of Labor Statistics and industry surveys. — Provides direct causal evidence on whether wage hikes above a cost-effectiveness threshold lead to measurable increases in automation (e.g., self-service kiosks, automated ordering) and corresponding reductions in low-skilled employment, controlling for demand elasticity.

[PATH:theoretical] Firm-level cost-benefit simulation models parameterized with wage, automation technology costs, and labor productivity data from service-sector firms in regions with varying minimum wages. — Tests the mechanistic condition that automation substitution occurs only when wage increases make the net present value of automation investment positive. This can identify the threshold wage level and confirm the hypothesized mechanism.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing empirical studies on minimum wage and employment effects, filtered by studies that explicitly measure automation or technology adoption as a mediating variable (e.g., Acemoglu & Restrepo, Autor, Dube & Lindner). — Synthesizes prior evidence across contexts to assess whether the automation substitution effect is consistently observed in high-demand-elasticity service sectors, and to evaluate the disputed status of the hypothesis.

scope.domain: local service-sector labor markets with high demand elasticity

qualifier.mechanism: increased labor costs accelerate investment in automation technologies for routine service tasks
qualifier.condition: when the wage increase exceeds the threshold that makes automation cost-effective relative to human labor

C006.subject: Raising the minimum wage in regions with strong service-sector demand
C006.object: low-skilled employment levels due to increased labor costs

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies of recent minimum wage increases in U.S. urban metro areas (e.g., Seattle, San Francisco, Chicago) using synthetic control or difference-in-differences methods, focusing on service-sector employment within 12 months post-implementation. — Directly tests the short-term effect in the specified geographic and sectoral scope, leveraging natural variation in policy implementation to isolate causal impact on low-skilled employment.

[PATH:theoretical] Labor demand elasticity estimates from meta-analyses or panel data for high-service-concentration urban markets, particularly for low-skilled roles in food service, retail, and hospitality. — If demand elasticity is high, the hypothesis predicts stronger negative employment effects; empirical elasticity estimates can validate or challenge the assumed mechanism of increased labor costs reducing employment.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal establishment-level data from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) or Bureau of Labor Statistics, tracking employment counts and hours in low-wage service sectors before and after minimum wage changes in high-demand urban areas. — Provides granular, high-frequency data to detect short-term employment adjustments, controlling for local economic conditions, and can distinguish between job loss and hour reduction effects.

scope.domain: local service-sector labor markets with high demand elasticity

qualifier.geographic: urban metropolitan areas in the United States with above-average service-sector employment concentration

C007.object: low-skilled employment levels when automation substitution costs exceed wage increases
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in regions with strong service-sector demand low-skilled employment levels when automation substitution costs exceed wage increases]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies of minimum wage increases in U.S. states with high service-sector density (e.g., Florida, Nevada), comparing employment changes in firms with high vs. low automation capital costs — Directly tests the hypothesis by examining whether low-skilled employment rises when wage hikes are smaller than automation substitution costs, exploiting variation in automation feasibility across firms.

[PATH:empirical] Firm-level survey data on automation adoption decisions in response to minimum wage changes (e.g., from the Bureau of Labor Statistics or industry-specific surveys of fast-food and retail firms) — Captures the mechanism by measuring whether firms that face high automation costs (e.g., small restaurants) retain or hire more low-skilled workers after a wage increase, relative to firms with low automation costs.

[PATH:theoretical] Dynamic labor-demand models incorporating firm heterogeneity in automation capital and demand elasticity (e.g., Acemoglu & Restrepo 2018 framework extended to minimum wage policy) — Provides a formal test of the hypothesis's key assumptions (low demand elasticity, capital constraints) and generates predictions about employment thresholds that can be compared with empirical data.

scope.domain: service-sector firms with thin profit margins or automation potential

qualifier.mechanism: when the cost of automating tasks (e.g., installing self-service kiosks) is higher than the marginal wage increase, firms maintain or expand low-skilled employment to meet demand, counteracting substitution effects
qualifier.tension: assumes demand elasticity for services is low and automation adoption is capital-constrained in the short term

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies comparing employment trends in U.S. cities that enacted minimum wage increases during economic expansions (e.g., Seattle, San Francisco) vs. matched control cities with no increases, focusing on service-sector employment and local consumer spending data. — Directly tests the causal claim under the specified temporal and geographic conditions, using high-frequency data to isolate the consumer spending channel.

[PATH:theoretical] Micro-simulations using input-output models calibrated to urban service economies (e.g., IMPLAN or REMI) that estimate the employment effects of minimum wage hikes through increased local demand. — Models the hypothesized chain from wage increase to consumer spending to low-skilled employment, allowing sensitivity analysis under varying demand elasticities and expansionary conditions.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage studies that include moderator variables for economic cycle (expansion vs. recession) and geographic demand strength (e.g., urban service-sector concentration). — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether the hypothesized positive effect is consistently observed in the qualified scope, controlling for publication bias and study design heterogeneity.

qualifier.geographic: in urban areas of developed economies with strong service-sector demand

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental analysis of minimum wage changes in high-demand service-sector MSAs (e.g., Seattle, San Francisco) using linked employer-employee data, with firms stratified by Lerner index or profit margin quintiles — Directly tests the predicted sign reversal by comparing employment changes at high- vs. low-market-power firms within the same local labor market, controlling for demand shocks.

[PATH:theoretical] Structural estimation of a model with firm heterogeneity in market power (e.g., oligopolistic competition with differentiated products) and minimum wage pass-through, calibrated to service-sector data — Evaluates the mechanism's internal consistency and quantifies conditions under which the net employment effect flips sign, informing whether the hypothesis is theoretically plausible.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage employment studies that report heterogeneous effects by firm size, concentration, or markup (e.g., Cengiz et al. 2019 re-analysis by firm profitability) — Synthesizes existing evidence to see if the predicted pattern (positive for high market power, negative for low) is already present in published results but obscured by pooling, providing a low-cost initial confirmation or refutation.

scope.domain: firm-level employment within high-demand service-sector local labor markets, segmented by firm market power

qualifier.mechanism: high-market-power firms absorb the wage cost by reducing profits and expand hiring due to demand, while low-market-power firms pass costs to consumers or cut hours/headcount
qualifier.tension: existing models treat firm heterogeneity as noise; this hypothesis predicts a systematic sign reversal based on market power
